finalText:
**Merge** creates a new commit that joins two branch histories together, keeping both branches' commits intact and adding a merge commit with two parents.

**Rebase** replays your branch's commits one-by-one onto the tip of another branch, producing new commits (new hashes) and a linear history — no merge commit.

Key differences:
- **History shape**: merge preserves the true, branching history (what actually happened, when); rebase rewrites it into a straight line (as if you'd branched off more recently).
- **Commit identity**: rebase changes commit hashes since it creates new commits; merge doesn't touch existing commits.
- **Safety on shared branches**: rebasing commits that others have already pulled rewrites history they depend on, causing pain (duplicate commits, conflicts) when they pull again. Merging is always safe for shared branches.
- **Conflict resolution**: merge resolves conflicts once, in a single commit. Rebase can make you resolve the same conflict repeatedly, once per replayed commit.

When to use each:
- **Rebase** your own local/feature branch onto `main` before opening a PR, to keep history clean and linear — as long as no one else is working off your branch yet.
- **Merge** when integrating a finished feature branch into `main`/`develop`, or any time the branch is shared/public — you want an accurate record and don't want to rewrite commits others have.
- A common workflow: rebase your feature branch locally to keep it current and tidy, then merge (often via PR, possibly squash-merge) into the main branch.

Rule of thumb: **never rebase commits that have been pushed and shared with others**, unless the whole team knows and coordinates around it.
